body: Can you explain why if you've got it setup declaratively (via commandfor/popovertarget) why would you be using the JS APIs? I thought they were mainly used for more complex scenarios (like interest based tooltips)?
@lukewarlow You might have some alternative way to invoke the popover, but you still want it associated with its invoker button.

Example: You have a popover that's attached to a toolbar button or something. It's normally activated by the button it's visually anchored to, but there are some alternative UI that also activates it. It should still be positioned the same way no matter how it's activated.

But despite using the attribute, it doesn't position correctly when you call showPopover(), so you decide to just use CSS anchoring from now on. It seems simpler than using both an attribute _and_ JS to fish for the correct HTML element reference to pass in. But then that fails to set up the semantic relationship properly...

I think we need the right thing to be easy if we want authors to do the right thing. The page already knows what the invoker is. Why should the author need to DIY this connection in JS?

> If there is only one possible invoker on the page (i.e. only one element with its `popovertarget` set to this popover's ID), can we default the `source` argument to that element? (It would still be possible to set it to null explicitly, if that was actually intended.)

That seems rather magical and unusual.

> If there is only one possible invoker on the page (i.e. only one element with its `popovertarget` set to this popover's ID), can we default the `source` argument to that element? (It would still be possible to set it to null explicitly, if that was actually intended.)

In addition to a button with the attributes, one could still have a button _without_ the required attributes that can show the popover from script, so that wouldn’t work here.

This also would not work when calling `.showPopover()` when – for example – hovering a link as the “invoker” here is not a button at all (nor an activation of some sorts).

> The page already knows what the invoker is. Why should the author need to DIY this connection in JS?

With the “hover a link and show a popover”-pattern, the page doesn’t know what the invoker is … unless you mean that it somehow tracks back which element the script-call originated from?

I think a first possible step here could for tooling to warn about an unset `source` _(although that might already be too much, because folks aren’t doing anything wrong here, as it is entirely optional)_.

I'm torn on this one but ultimately I don't think we should be setting automagical semantic relationships when using JS to open a popover. A popover might not have any invoker. For example, what if you wanted a one-time dismissible popover to appear on the page before the user interacts with the page?

It makes sense to create the relationship declaratively with `popovertarget` or `commandfor` but when the user chooses to use script, there is usually a more complex usecase or simple reason like the example above. I also don't think warning in DevTools is correct for every unset source because there are legitimate usecases where you don't have a source. One option that might work is to create this relationship in the case that there is an event listener for a click/toggle on an element that triggers the popover. But again, this could get it wrong.

I don't think we should implement this as it has some potentially surprising consequences, which developers _may_ not immediately realise:

 - Setting the popover source will change the focus mode of the popover (popovers with invokers act like focus groups, as opposed to popovers without invokers).
 - The button will establish an accessible relationship with the popover. 

These sound like reasonable things but if the relationship is implicit (rather than explicit through `popovertarget` or `{source}`) then these behaviours silently change, in ways which might be surprising to a developer, especially as accessibility testing is often overlooked.

I understand that OP mentions this is resolvable by using `{source:null}` but that seems brittle for two reasons:

1. If a developer explicitly does _not_ want these behaviours, they have to understand that they can pass `null` and that that has a different meaning to `{source:undefined}`.
2. Subsequent developers who might be in the same area of code need to look at `{source:null}` and recognise that this has semantic meaning, and _not remove it_. I can easily imagine a developer "cleaning up" code like this which would cause a regression in behaviour on a website.

Generally, I agree with the comments here that this sounds more confusing than the existing situation. And magically using the idref-based relationship from `popovertarget` or `commandfor` seems way too magical. It's possible that a button triggers a popover via `popovertarget` or `commandfor`, but then script re-uses that same popover for other purposes, triggered by other elements. It'd be incorrect and weird in that case to still hook it up to the first button.

Yes, it's possible to "forget" to add a source, but typically the immediate effect is that your anchor positioning doesn't work as you expect, and you realize you forgot the source. It's possible you're also not using anchor positioning, so in that case only the focus behavior and a11y relationships are missing, which is harder to see. There are certainly use cases for showing a popover without a source, so I think it'd be too much console spam to always warn if `source` is missing. Perhaps there's the one corner case that might be impactful:
 - developer called `showPopover()` without a `source`.
 - CSS calls for an anchor relationship (uses `anchor()` or `position-area`).
 - CSS does *not* define an `anchor-name` or `position-anchor`, so it's written kind of to expect an implicit relationship

I'm a bit skeptical here too. Even that might be annoying, I'm not sure. It also might be a bit hard to implement.

The CSS Working Group just discussed `Forgetting source argument to showPopover() is too easy`.

Thinking some more on that commandForElement thing I mentioned at the end I don't think you even can always get all invokers for a popover, because that works cross tree and we can't add a getter that exposes shadow tree contents...

But then having a getter that returns "all the invokers for this element, but oops not quite" also doesn't feel quite right. I think the source attribute is good because you use it with a specific element you have in mind. Adding the getter for invokers that you then have to think about isn't necessarily any better.

I'm curious what the actual concerns are with the querySelector('button[commandfor="' + id + '"]') case. @keithamus can you explain that attack vector a bit more?

> I'm curious what the actual concerns are with the querySelector('button[commandfor="' + id + '"]') case. [@keithamus](https://github.com/keithamus) can you explain that attack vector a bit more?

Sure, in some cases the `id` might be from, for example, user generated content so it's a potential vector for injection. The severity depends a lot, of course. It might not be an actual risk, but there are automated tools (or even just lints) that will ban codebases from using concatenation in `querySelector` for this reason. I don't think there's a specific gotcha but it detracts enough from the ergonomics to at least consider an alternative.
